evidence: Knuckles said in interviews, including with Red Bull Music Academy, that his first drum machine was a TR-909 that reached him from Derrick May in Detroit in 1984, and that May came down to show him how to program it. Whether it was sold or given is told both ways, including by people present at the time. Wikipedia's article on Knuckles gives the purchase as around 1983, and says he played the Warehouse until November 1982, when he started his own club, the Power Plant; so on either date the machine arrived after the Warehouse years.

earlier.title: TR-909, as a rhythm composer for musicians

trackPair.whatToListenFor: Do this as a comparison. Put on a Philadelphia disco record from 1976 and listen to the drums: a person playing, pushing slightly ahead in the chorus, dragging in the verse. Then put on a Chicago house record from 1986. The kick is in exactly the same place in every bar for seven minutes, and above it there is a short, bright, ringing open hi-hat that never varies either. That machine hi-hat, laid under records that were never built for it, is what a night at the Power Plant turned into.

explanation: Knuckles got his first drum machine, a Roland 909, from Derrick May in Detroit. Accounts differ on whether May sold it to him or gave it to him, and on the year: 1984 in Knuckles's own interviews, around 1983 in others. Either way it came after he had left the Warehouse for his own club, the Power Plant, in late 1982, so the Warehouse, which named the genre, was a room without a drum machine. He used it live, playing a steady machine beat underneath disco and soul records, which kept the floor moving through the parts of a record where the drums thin out. The 909 entered Chicago as a DJ's tool for stretching old records, not as a studio instrument for making new ones, and that order, live first and studio second, is a big part of why house records are built the way they are. House music starts in that gap between an old record and a drum machine holding it up.
